{{Short description|Mathematical tool for summing arithmetic functions}}
[[File:Dirichlet hyperbola example_4.svg|thumb|An example of the Dirichlet hyperbola method with <math>n = 10,</math> <math>a \approx 2.7,</math> and <math>b \approx 3.7.</math>]]

In [[number theory]], the '''Dirichlet hyperbola method''' is a technique to evaluate the sum

: <math>F(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n f(k)</math>.

The first step is to find a pair of functions {{Mvar|g}} and {{Mvar|h}} such that, using [[Dirichlet convolution]], we have {{Math|1=''f'' = ''g'' &lowast; ''h''}}; the sum then becomes

: <math>F(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{xy=k}^{} g(x) h(y),</math>

where the inner sum runs over all ordered pairs {{Math|(''x'',''y'')}} of positive [[integers]] such that {{Math|1=''xy'' = ''k''}}.  In the [[Cartesian plane]], these pairs lie on a [[hyperbola]], and when the double sum is fully expanded, there is a [[bijection]] between the terms of the sum and the [[lattice points]] in the first quadrant on the hyperbolas of the form {{Math|1=''xy'' = ''k''}}, where {{Mvar|k}} runs over the integers {{Math|1 &le; ''k'' &le; ''n''}}: for each such point {{Math|(''x'',''y'')}}, the sum contains a term {{Math|''g''(''x'')''h''(''y'')}}, and vice versa.

Let {{Mvar|a}} be a real number, not necessarily an integer, such that {{Math|1 < ''a'' < ''n''}}, and let {{Math|1=''b'' = ''n''/''a''}}.  Then the lattice points can be split into three overlapping regions: one region is bounded by {{Math|1 &le; ''x'' &le; ''a''}} and {{Math|1 &le; ''y'' &le; ''n''/''x''}}, another region is bounded by {{Math|1 &le; ''y'' &le; ''b''}} and {{Math|1 &le; ''x'' &le; ''n''/''y''}}, and the third is bounded by {{Math|1 &le; ''x'' &le; ''a''}} and {{Math|1 &le; ''y'' &le; ''b''}}.  In the diagram, the first region is the [[union (set theory)|union]] of the blue and red regions, the second region is the union of the red and green, and the third region is the red.  Note that this third region is the [[intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of the first two regions.  By the [[principle of inclusion and exclusion]], the full sum is therefore the sum over the first region, plus the sum over the second region, minus the sum over the third region.  This yields the formula<ref>{{cite book |last1=Apostol |first1=Tom M. |title=Introduction to analytic number theory |date=1976 |publisher=Springer-Verlag |location=New York |isbn=0-387-90163-9 |page=69}}</ref>

{{NumBlk|:|<math>
\begin{align}
F(n) &= \sum_{k=1}^n f(k)  \\
    &= \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{xy=k}^{} g(x)h(y)  \\
    &= \sum_{x=1}^a \sum_{y=1}^{n/x} g(x)h(y) + \sum_{y=1}^b \sum_{x=1}^{n/y} g(x)h(y) - \sum_{x=1}^a \sum_{y=1}^b g(x)h(y)  \text{.}\end{align}
</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

== Examples ==

Let {{Math|''&sigma;''<sub>0</sub>(''n'')}} be the [[Divisor function|divisor-counting function]], and let {{Math|''D''(''n'')}} be [[Divisor summatory function|its summatory function]]:

: <math>D(n) = \sum_{k=1}^n \sigma_0(k).</math>

Computing {{Math|''D''(''n'')}} naïvely requires [[integer factorization|factoring]] every integer in the interval {{Math|[1, ''n'']}}; an improvement can be made by using a modified [[Sieve of Eratosthenes]], but this still requires {{Math|''Õ''(''n'')}} [[Big O notation#Extensions to the Bachmann–Landau notations|time]].  Since {{Math|''&sigma;''<sub>0</sub>}} admits the Dirichlet convolution {{Math|1=''&sigma;''<sub>0</sub> = 1 &lowast; 1}}, taking {{Math|1=''a'' = ''b'' = {{radic|''n''}}}} in ({{EquationNote|1}}) yields the formula

: <math>D(n) = \sum_{x=1}^{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{y=1}^{n/x} 1 \cdot 1 + \sum_{y=1}^{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{x=1}^{n/y} 1 \cdot 1 - \sum_{x=1}^{\sqrt{n}} \sum_{y=1}^{\sqrt{n}} 1 \cdot 1,</math>

which simplifies to
: <math>D(n) = 2 \cdot \sum_{x=1}^{\sqrt{n}} \left\lfloor \frac{n}{x} \right\rfloor - \left\lfloor \sqrt{n} \right\rfloor^2,</math>
which can be evaluated in {{Math|''O''({{radic|''n''}})}} operations.

The method also has theoretical applications: for example, [[Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet]] introduced the technique in 1849 to obtain the estimate<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dirichlet |first=Peter Gustav Lejeune |author-link=Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet |date=1849 |title=Über die Bestimmung der mittleren Werthe in der Zahlentheorie |url=https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k994363/f59.item |journal=Abhandlungen der Königlich Preussischen Akademie der Wissenchaften |language=German |pages=49–66 |via=Gallica}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Tenenbaum |first=Gérald |author-link=Gérald Tenenbaum |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=UEk-CgAAQBAJ&dq=dirichlet+hyperbola+method&pg=PR15 |title=Introduction to Analytic and Probabilistic Number Theory |date=2015-07-16 |publisher=American Mathematical Soc. |isbn=9780821898543 |location= |pages=44 |language=en}}</ref>

: <math>D(n) = n \log n + (2\gamma - 1)n + O(\sqrt{n}),</math>

where {{Mvar|&gamma;}} is the [[Euler–Mascheroni constant]].
